concepts.def: Spontaneous uprising in Petrograd (8 March NS / 23 Feb OS) caused by bread shortages; Tsar Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March.
Liberal-led government (March-Oct 1917) committed to continuing WWI; Prince Lvov then Kerensky led it.
Coexistence of Provisional Government and Petrograd Soviet; Lenin's slogan was 'All power to the Soviets'.
April 1917 program calling for socialist revolution, end to WWI, no Provisional Government, land to peasants.
Bolshevik seizure of power on 25 October OS / 7 November NS in Petrograd; storming of Winter Palace.
Red Army (Bolsheviks) vs White Army plus foreign intervention; Reds won via War Communism, Cheka terror, central control.

mcqs.q: Which Bolshevik slogan summarised Lenin's April Theses?
What was the immediate cause of the February Revolution?

numericals.q: In what year did the Russian Civil War end?

free_texts.q: Who led the Bolsheviks during the October Revolution?
free_texts.hint: Vladimir Ilyich, returned from Switzerland in April 1917.

concepts.def: Stalin outmanoeuvred Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin after Lenin's death to become sole leader by 1929.
Rapid industrialisation programmes starting 1928; heavy industry, steel, coal targets set by Gosplan; first plan completed in four years.
Forced merging of peasant farms into kolkhozes from 1929; led to dekulakisation and the Ukrainian famine Holodomor 1932-33.
Mass purges including Moscow Show Trials of Old Bolsheviks; NKVD under Yezhov; estimated 700,000 executed.
Propaganda-driven worship of Stalin as Vozhd; controlled art, cinema (Eisenstein), education and history-writing.
USSR's WWII 1941-45 following Operation Barbarossa; Stalingrad 1942-43 turning point; ended with Berlin's fall May 1945.

mcqs.q: Which 1932-33 famine resulted from collectivisation policies in Ukraine?
Who headed the NKVD during the height of the Great Terror?

numericals.q: In what year did Stalin die?

free_texts.q: What name was given to Stalin's forced farm-merging policy?
free_texts.hint: Peasant land merged into kolkhozes from 1929.

concepts.def: Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949 after defeating Chiang Kai-shek's GMD.
Redistribution of land from landlords to peasants; an estimated one million landlords executed in struggle sessions.
Brief liberalisation inviting criticism, followed by Anti-Rightist crackdown when criticism grew too sharp.
Mass mobilisation for industrial and agricultural transformation through communes and backyard furnaces; caused famine killing 15-45 million.
Mao's campaign against bourgeois elements using Red Guards; targeted Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping and the 'Four Olds'.
Faction led by Jiang Qing (Mao's wife) that drove Cultural Revolution policies; arrested October 1976 after Mao's death.

mcqs.q: Which campaign caused the famine of 1959-61 in China?
Who led the Gang of Four?

numericals.q: In what year did Mao Zedong die?

free_texts.q: What youth movement enforced the Cultural Revolution?
free_texts.hint: Student paramilitaries waving Mao's Little Red Book.

concepts.def: Failed Nazi coup in Bavaria on 8-9 November 1923; Hitler imprisoned at Landsberg and wrote Mein Kampf.
Nazi vote rose from 2.6% (1928) to 18.3% (1930) to 37.3% (July 1932) amid Great Depression collapse.
Papen and Hindenburg's circle persuaded the President to appoint Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933.
Burning blamed on communist van der Lubbe; Reichstag Fire Decree suspended civil liberties allowing mass arrests.
Law passed 23 March 1933 granting Hitler power to legislate without Reichstag; Centre Party voted in favour.
30 June - 2 July 1934 purge of SA leadership including Ernst Rohm by SS; secured Hitler's hold on military and party.

mcqs.q: On what date did Hitler become Chancellor of Germany?
Whose SA leadership was purged in 1934?

numericals.q: What percentage did the NSDAP win in the July 1932 Reichstag election?

free_texts.q: Which 1923 event landed Hitler in Landsberg prison?
free_texts.hint: Munich coup attempt of November 1923.

concepts.def: Kiel sailors' mutiny led to Kaiser Wilhelm II's abdication on 9 November 1918 and proclamation of a republic by Scheidemann.
Drafted by Hugo Preuss; established proportional representation, universal suffrage, and Article 48 emergency powers for the President.
Ruhr occupation by France triggered passive resistance and money printing; one US dollar reached 4.2 trillion marks in November 1923.
Foreign minister Gustav Stresemann negotiated Dawes Plan 1924, Locarno 1925 and League entry 1926; period of relative stability.
Communist revolt led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht in Berlin; crushed by Freikorps; both leaders murdered.
Emergency clause allowing Presidential rule by decree; used heavily 1930-33 under Bruning, Papen, Schleicher then Hitler.

mcqs.q: Who led the Spartacist Uprising of January 1919?
Which 1924 plan rescheduled German reparations?

numericals.q: In what year did hyperinflation peak in Weimar Germany?

free_texts.q: Which constitutional article allowed rule by emergency decree?
free_texts.hint: Used heavily by Bruning, Papen and Hitler.

concepts.def: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreed on UN, German occupation zones, free Polish elections; tensions over Eastern Europe.
Truman, Attlee and Stalin; disagreements over reparations and Poland; Truman hinted at atomic bomb.
George Kennan's February 1946 cable from Moscow analysing Soviet expansionism; basis for containment policy.
March 1947 pledge to support free peoples resisting subjugation; $400 million aid to Greece and Turkey.
European Recovery Program; $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe; rejected by Stalin for Eastern bloc.
Stalin blocked land access to West Berlin; West responded with airlift delivering 2.3 million tons of supplies.

mcqs.q: Who authored the Long Telegram of 1946?
What was the Western response to the 1948 Berlin Blockade?

numericals.q: In what year was NATO founded?

free_texts.q: What 1947 doctrine pledged US aid against communism?
free_texts.hint: Named after the US President; aid to Greece and Turkey.

concepts.def: Failed CIA-backed invasion of Cuba by exiles; humiliated Kennedy and pushed Castro closer to USSR.
On 14 October a U-2 flight photographed Soviet SS-4 medium-range ballistic missile sites in Cuba.
Kennedy's Executive Committee of the National Security Council; debated airstrike vs blockade options 16-28 October.
Kennedy announced naval blockade of Cuba on television; Soviet ships turned back on 24 October.
Secret deal 28 October: Soviets withdrew missiles in Cuba; US publicly pledged no invasion, secretly removed Jupiters from Turkey.
Direct Moscow-Washington teletype link established June 1963 to prevent miscommunication during nuclear crises.

mcqs.q: What surveillance aircraft photographed Cuban missile sites?
Which secret concession did Kennedy make to end the crisis?

numericals.q: How many days did the Cuban Missile Crisis officially last?

free_texts.q: Who led the USSR during the Cuban Missile Crisis?
free_texts.hint: Soviet First Secretary; later ousted in 1964.

concepts.def: West German Chancellor Willy Brandt's policy from 1969 normalising relations with Eastern Europe; Moscow and Warsaw treaties 1970.
Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty signed by Nixon and Brezhnev in May 1972; froze ICBM launchers and included ABM Treaty.
February 1972 visit broke 22 years of US-PRC estrangement; Kissinger's secret diplomacy in 1971 prepared it.
Signed by 35 states in August 1975; recognised post-war borders, pledged cooperation, included human rights Basket III.
Treaty signed June 1979 by Carter and Brezhnev limiting strategic launchers; not ratified by US Senate after Afghanistan invasion.
Red Army entered Afghanistan 24 December 1979 to support Karmal regime; ended detente and triggered Carter Doctrine.

mcqs.q: Who pursued Ostpolitik from 1969 as West German Chancellor?
Which 1975 conference produced the Final Act with human rights provisions?

numericals.q: In what year did Nixon visit the People's Republic of China?

free_texts.q: Which 1972 treaty limited strategic missiles?
free_texts.hint: First Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty.

concepts.def: New General Secretary launched perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness); accelerated Soviet decline.
Reagan and Gorbachev signed Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty 8 December 1987; eliminated 500-5,500 km missiles.
Gorbachev's renunciation of Brezhnev Doctrine; Eastern bloc states free to choose 'their way' without Soviet intervention.
GDR opened crossings on 9 November 1989 after Schabowski's confused press conference; symbolic collapse of bloc.
Two-plus-Four Treaty September 1990 led to unification on 3 October 1990 under Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Belavezha Accords 8 December 1991 dissolved USSR; Gorbachev resigned 25 December; Soviet flag lowered over Kremlin.

mcqs.q: What Russian terms describe Gorbachev's openness and restructuring?
Which 1987 treaty eliminated intermediate-range nuclear missiles?

numericals.q: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?

free_texts.q: Who succeeded Chernenko as Soviet leader in 1985?
free_texts.hint: Launched perestroika and glasnost.

concepts.def: Supreme Court unanimous decision authored by Earl Warren overturning Plessy v Ferguson; declared school segregation unconstitutional.
381-day boycott sparked by Rosa Parks' arrest 1 December 1955; led by Martin Luther King Jr; ended with Browder v Gayle ruling.
Nine Black students integrated Central High; Eisenhower sent 101st Airborne after Governor Faubus deployed National Guard.
250,000 gathered at Lincoln Memorial 28 August 1963; King delivered 'I Have a Dream' speech.
Signed by Lyndon B Johnson 2 July 1964; outlawed discrimination based on race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.
Followed Selma to Montgomery marches; banned literacy tests and authorised federal supervision of registration in Southern states.

mcqs.q: Which 1954 Supreme Court ruling overturned segregated schooling?
Whose arrest in Montgomery sparked the 1955 bus boycott?

numericals.q: In what year was the Voting Rights Act signed?

free_texts.q: Who delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963?
free_texts.hint: Baptist minister and SCLC leader.

concepts.def: Movement advocating African unity; fifth Pan-African Congress 1945 in Manchester featured Nkrumah, Kenyatta and Du Bois.
Kwame Nkrumah led Gold Coast to independence on 6 March 1957; first sub-Saharan African colony to break free from Britain.
Seventeen African states gained independence in 1960 including Nigeria, Senegal, Cameroon and the Congo.
FLN-led struggle against France; Battle of Algiers 1956-57; ended with Evian Accords March 1962 and de Gaulle's recognition.
Kikuyu-led insurgency in British Kenya; brutal counter-insurgency in detention camps; Kenyatta became President in 1964.
Founded 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 states under Haile Selassie; promoted unity and decolonisation.

mcqs.q: Who led Ghana to independence in 1957?
Which 1962 accords ended the Algerian War?

numericals.q: How many African states gained independence in the Year of Africa?

free_texts.q: What 1963 organisation united African states in Addis Ababa?
free_texts.hint: Organisation of African Unity; predecessor to the AU.

concepts.def: Founded 1885; became mass independence movement under Gandhi from 1920; Nehru emerged as principal political heir.
Gandhi's 240-mile march to Dandi in March-April 1930 challenging the British salt monopoly; key satyagraha campaign.
League led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah; Lahore Resolution 1940 demanded separate Muslim state; basis for Pakistan.
Congress declared 'Do or Die' on 8 August 1942 demanding immediate British withdrawal; leaders jailed for the war.
Last Viceroy Lord Louis Mountbatten announced partition on 3 June 1947; Radcliffe drew boundary in five weeks.
India and Pakistan independent; up to 15 million displaced and 1-2 million killed in communal violence in Punjab and Bengal.

mcqs.q: Who led the Muslim League and articulated the Two-Nation Theory?
Which 1930 campaign challenged the British salt monopoly?

numericals.q: In what year was British India partitioned?

free_texts.q: Who became India's first Prime Minister in 1947?
free_texts.hint: Congress leader; daughter Indira later became PM.

concepts.def: Viet Minh under Ho Chi Minh and Giap defeated French forces at Dien Bien Phu May 1954; Geneva Accords partitioned Vietnam at 17th parallel.
Sukarno declared independence 17 August 1945; armed struggle against Dutch ended with Round Table Conference December 1949.
British counter-insurgency against MCP guerrillas; Briggs Plan resettlement of 500,000 Chinese into New Villages.
United States granted independence 4 July 1946 under Tydings-McDuffie Act timetable; Manuel Roxas first president.
29 Asian and African states met April 1955 in Indonesia; Sukarno, Nehru, Nasser, Zhou Enlai promoted Non-Aligned Movement.
Conflict between North Vietnamese DRV and US-backed South Vietnam; Tet Offensive 1968; fall of Saigon 30 April 1975.

mcqs.q: Where did the Viet Minh decisively defeat France in 1954?
Which 1955 conference launched the Non-Aligned Movement?

numericals.q: In what year did Saigon fall to North Vietnamese forces?

free_texts.q: Who declared Indonesian independence in August 1945?
free_texts.hint: First President of Indonesia; ousted by Suharto 1967.

concepts.def: Economic crisis, weak democratic institutions, defeat or humiliation in war and charismatic leadership common to Mussolini, Hitler, Stalin and Mao.
Fascism (Mussolini), National Socialism (Hitler), Marxism-Leninism (Stalin), Maoism — each provided justifying doctrine and mass mobilisation.
Goebbels' Reich Ministry, Mussolini's Minculpop, Soviet socialist realism and Maoist little red book shaped public consciousness.
Gestapo, OVRA, NKVD and Public Security Bureau combined informers, secret police and forced-labour camps to crush opposition.
Autarky in Italy and Germany; Five-Year Plans under Stalin; Great Leap and collectivisation under Mao.
Expansionism via Abyssinia 1935, Anschluss 1938, Polish invasion 1939, Korean War involvement and Sino-Soviet split 1960.

mcqs.q: Which secret police force served Mussolini's regime?
Which artistic doctrine prevailed in Stalin's USSR?

numericals.q: In what year did Mussolini march on Rome?

free_texts.q: What name describes Mussolini's Italian ideology?
free_texts.hint: From Latin fasces; emerged in Italy 1919-22.

causes-second-world-war.topic_display: Causes of the Second World War

concepts.def: Diktat resentment, Article 231 war guilt, reparations and the loss of 13% of German territory fuelled revisionism.
League of Nations failed to deter Japan in Manchuria 1931 and Italy in Abyssinia 1935; Hoare-Laval Pact discredited it.
Lebensraum, rearmament 1935, Rhineland 1936, Anschluss 1938 and Sudetenland 1938 progressively dismantled Versailles.
British and French policy reaching its peak at Munich Conference September 1938 with Chamberlain's 'peace for our time' claim.
Ribbentrop and Molotov signed non-aggression pact with secret protocols dividing Poland and the Baltics.
Germany invaded 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war 3 September; Soviet invasion from east 17 September.

mcqs.q: Which 1938 conference ceded the Sudetenland to Germany?
Who signed the 1939 non-aggression pact for the USSR?

numericals.q: In what month and year did Hitler remilitarise the Rhineland?

free_texts.q: What British PM signed the Munich Agreement in 1938?
free_texts.hint: Conservative; held the umbrella aloft on return.

concepts.def: September 1935 laws stripped German Jews of citizenship; Reich Citizenship Law and Law for the Protection of German Blood.
Pogrom 9-10 November 1938 in Germany and Austria; 267 synagogues destroyed, 30,000 Jews sent to camps.
Mobile killing squads operating behind Wehrmacht lines in USSR; killed 1.5 million Jews including Babi Yar massacre September 1941.
Reinhard Heydrich coordinated Final Solution with 15 senior officials on 20 January 1942 at Wannsee villa.
Six extermination centres in occupied Poland including Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor; used Zyklon B and carbon monoxide.
Approximately 6 million Jews murdered, including 1.5 million children; also targeted Roma, Soviet POWs, disabled and political prisoners.

mcqs.q: Where did Heydrich coordinate the Final Solution in January 1942?
Which gas was used at Auschwitz-Birkenau?

numericals.q: Approximately how many Jews were murdered in the Holocaust (millions)?

free_texts.q: Which largest death camp lay in occupied southern Poland?
free_texts.hint: Birkenau (Auschwitz II) was its largest sub-camp.

concepts.def: Established by London Charter 8 August 1945; four judges from US, UK, USSR and France presided over major Nazi leaders.
Conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity; novel framework codifying Nuremberg Principles.
Goering, Hess, Ribbentrop, Keitel, Streicher and 19 others; 12 sentenced to death, 7 to prison, 3 acquitted.
US Chief Prosecutor and Associate Supreme Court Justice; delivered famous opening 21 November 1945 framing the moral case.
Court declined arguments that Allied conduct (Katyn, Dresden, Hiroshima) excused Nazi crimes; established individual responsibility.
ILC codified 1950; influenced Genocide Convention 1948, Geneva Conventions 1949 and ICC Statute 1998.

mcqs.q: Who served as US Chief Prosecutor at Nuremberg?
How many major Nazi defendants were sentenced to death by the IMT?

numericals.q: In what year did the IMT verdict at Nuremberg conclude?

free_texts.q: Which 1948 UN convention was inspired by Nuremberg?
free_texts.hint: Drafted partly by Raphael Lemkin who coined the term.

concepts.def: Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy 1882) and Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain 1907) created bloc rivalry.
Anglo-German naval race after 1898 Tirpitz Plan; conscript armies and Schlieffen Plan increased pressure for mobilisation.
First Moroccan Crisis 1905-06 and Agadir 1911 inflamed Franco-German relations; Balkan competition between Austria and Russia.
Pan-Slavism backed Serbia; Bosnian annexation 1908 and Balkan Wars 1912-13 destabilised Ottoman successor states.
Gavrilo Princip of Black Hand killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand; July Crisis followed Austria's ultimatum to Serbia.
Austrian declaration on Serbia 28 July; Russian mobilisation; German declarations on Russia 1 August and France 3 August; Britain joined 4 August.

mcqs.q: Which secret Serbian group sponsored Princip in 1914?
Which crisis in 1911 inflamed Franco-German tensions?

numericals.q: In what year was the Triple Entente completed?

free_texts.q: Whose assassination triggered the July Crisis of 1914?
free_texts.hint: Heir to Austria-Hungary; killed in Sarajevo.

concepts.def: Opened 18 January 1919; Council of Four — Wilson (US), Lloyd George (UK), Clemenceau (France), Orlando (Italy) — dominated negotiations.
War guilt clause assigning Germany and her allies sole responsibility for losses; legal basis for reparations claims.
London Schedule of Payments April 1921 set 132 billion gold marks; reduced by Dawes 1924 and Young 1929 Plans.
Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France, Eupen-Malmedy to Belgium, Polish Corridor to Poland; all colonies became League mandates.
Army limited to 100,000, no conscription, no air force, navy limited to 6 battleships, Rhineland demilitarised.
January 1918 program included open diplomacy, self-determination and League of Nations; many points diluted in final treaty.

mcqs.q: Which clause assigned Germany sole war guilt?
What was the maximum size of Germany's army after Versailles?

numericals.q: How many points were in Wilson's January 1918 program?

free_texts.q: Which French leader at Paris demanded harsh terms?
free_texts.hint: Nicknamed Le Tigre; French Premier.

league-of-nations-failure.topic_display: Failure of the League of Nations

concepts.def: Part I of Treaty of Versailles 1919; created Assembly, Council and Secretariat in Geneva; collective security under Article 16.
Senate rejected Versailles in November 1919 and March 1920 over Lodge reservations; Wilson's stroke campaigning for ratification.
Mussolini bombarded Corfu after Italian general killed in Greece; Conference of Ambassadors handled it, undermining League.
Japan invaded Manchuria after Mukden Incident 18 September 1931; Lytton Report condemned Japan, which left the League March 1933.
Mussolini invaded Ethiopia October 1935; League sanctions excluded oil; Hoare-Laval Pact December 1935 destroyed League credibility.
Unanimity rule on Council, no standing army, slow procedures; relied on UK and French enforcement and economic sanctions.

mcqs.q: What 1935 secret pact undermined League credibility over Abyssinia?
Which 1931 incident triggered Japan's invasion of Manchuria?

numericals.q: In what year did Japan leave the League of Nations?

free_texts.q: In which Swiss city was the League headquartered?
free_texts.hint: Palace of Nations built 1929-38.
